faq.a: Rarely, but HIV‑related interstitial pneumonitis can mimic them in younger patients.
faq.q: Can IIPs occur in young adults?

faq.a: No; HRCT pattern plus exclusion of other causes is sufficient in most settings.
faq.q: Is a lung biopsy always needed?

faq.a: Limited to organizing pneumonia; they are not effective for UIP and may worsen infection risk.
faq.q: What is the role of steroids?

exam: A 55‑year‑old farmer presents with 6 months of dry cough and exertional dyspnoea; HRCT shows basal honey‑comb. What is the most likely diagnosis and next step? — Identify UIP pattern, diagnose idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, refer for antifibrotic therapy.
How would you differentiate idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis from pulmonary TB in a patient with chronic cough in a TB‑endemic area? — Emphasise HRCT pattern, sputum AFB, lack of systemic TB symptoms.

A patient with known HIV presents with progressive dyspnoea; CD4 = 350. HRCT shows diffuse ground‑glass. What diagnosis should you consider and why? — HIV‑related interstitial pneumonitis; CD4 may be preserved, imaging differs from UIP.
What are the key components of the GAP index and how does it guide management? — Gender, Age, FVC, DLCO; higher scores predict mortality and transplant referral.
Why are systemic steroids contraindicated in usual interstitial pneumonia? — They do not improve fibrosis and increase infection risk.
In a setting without HRCT, what bedside clues help suspect IIPs? — Insidious dyspnoea, bibasal Velcro crackles, clubbing, normal chest X‑ray early, exclusion of infection.
What acute complication of IIPs requires immediate ICU transfer? — Acute exacerbation with rapid hypoxaemia, often triggered by infection or embolism.
Explain why antifibrotic therapy is preferred over immunosuppression in UIP. — Targets fibroblast activity, slows decline; immunosuppression worsens outcomes.
ai.title: Idiopathic Interstitial Pneumonias
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Idiopathic interstitial pneumonias (IIPs) are a group of diffuse lung diseases causing progressive fibrosis. Diagnosis relies on pattern recognition, exclusion of known causes, and limited investigations in low‑resource settings.

b: Four major patterns: usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP), nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP), organizing pneumonia (OP), and desquamative interstitial pneumonia (DIP).
Most common in adults >50 y, but HIV, TB, and occupational exposures can mimic them in East Africa.
sections.p: IIPs are chronic, diffuse lung disorders of unknown cause that affect the interstitium and alveolar walls, leading to impaired gas exchange and eventual respiratory failure.

b: Diagnostic criteria: progressive dyspnoea, dry cough, restrictive spirometry, HRCT pattern, and lack of identifiable cause.
Severity staging uses GAP index (Gender, Age, Physiology) when pulmonary function tests (PFTs) are available.
sections.p: Think of IIPs as a diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out infection, connective‑tissue disease, drug toxicity, and environmental exposures.

b: Common mimics in low‑resource settings: pulmonary TB, HIV‑related lymphocytic interstitial pneumonitis, post‑malaria fibrosis.
Rapid deterioration may be triggered by infection, pulmonary embolism, or acute exacerbation.
sections.p: Patients present with insidious dyspnoea on exertion and a dry cough; early recognition can prevent unnecessary antibiotics and allow timely referral for antifibrotic therapy or lung transplant.

t.b: Is there a diffuse reticular pattern? → Suggests interstitial disease; if unavailable, rely on clinical pattern.
What is the radiologic pattern? → UIP (basal honey‑comb), NSIP (ground‑glass), OP (consolidation), DIP (diffuse ground‑glass).
Is there a restrictive defect? → FVC < 80 % predicted, normal or increased FEV1/FVC.
How much desaturation occurs? → Drop > 4 % or distance < 300 m indicates severe disease.

t.a: Basic labs (CBC, HIV test, sputum AFB)
t.b: Are infections excluded? → Positive TB or HIV changes diagnosis.

b: Antifibrotic agents (pirfenidone, nintedanib) slow progression; avoid in severe liver disease.
Supplemental oxygen for SpO₂ < 88 % at rest or on exertion.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause if identified; otherwise focus on antifibrotic therapy, oxygen, and supportive care.

b: TB: productive cough, night sweats, positive sputum; HRCT shows nodules, cavitation.
Heart failure: peripheral oedema, elevated JVP, cardiomegaly on X‑ray.
sections.p: Distinguish IIPs from TB, HIV‑related interstitial pneumonitis, and chronic heart failure.

b: HRCT may show ground‑glass that mimics infection; correlate with clinical course.
Spirometry can be normal in early disease; rely on symptoms and imaging.
sections.p: Normal chest X‑ray early in disease; HIV patients may have normal CD4 counts yet interstitial disease.

b: Ask about occupational dust, bird exposure, and herbal inhalants.
Check for clubbing – more common in UIP.
sections.p: Focus on pattern recognition, exclusion of common tropical infections, and pragmatic use of limited tests.

b: Treating presumed TB without microbiologic proof.
Delaying referral for antifibrotic therapy because of lack of PFTs.
sections.p: Avoid over‑reliance on antibiotics and missing the need for referral.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening of dyspnoea or new chest pain
Signs of acute respiratory failure (confusion, cyanosis)
